column2: “Naive!” Fingel rebuked him solemnly. “We can deny it, but we don't control the hearing. The final say belongs to the lifetime professors. If those old science geeks and old religious cranks think Chu Zihang was involved, it won't matter whether we admit it.”

“The best way to show Chu Zihang didn't do these things is to show someone else did.” One paparazzo evidently had a sound grasp of law. “The best way to prove a suspect innocent is to find the real culprit.”
“You mean frame someone?” another asked.
“You could put it that way, though that's rather coarse, not very refined.” The legal-minded paparazzo looked embarrassed.
“Refined, my ass! Who cares? As long as we win, that's what matters. It's a debate, just a matter of talking,” Fingel said. “Still, you have a point.”

“The problem is that ordinary people couldn't have done these things. They're clearly connected to hybrids or dragons.” A junior frowned. “If a lunatic like Chu Zihang didn't do them, some other lunatic must have. There aren't many people we could pin them on.”
“I know a group! They're perfect!” Fingel slapped his thigh, eyes blazing.

The download bar on the screen had passed ninety-five percent. Soon all the hidden files in Norma's storage would be backed up on Parsi's hard-drive array. No one could stop the backup, because no one had higher access than a white card. Inside Norma's network, a white-card holder flew like a god; the other users were ants crawling about, unaware that a god looked down on them.

Traffic in and out of the central control room suddenly began to rise again. The paparazzi seemed to have regrouped and thrown themselves enthusiastically back into work, unaware that Parsi was monitoring every stream of data.
Parsi tried switching to their interface to see what they were doing.

“Hi there. I don't know who you are, but unfortunately your access has to end. I'm sorry, but there's nothing I can do; someone with higher clearance has given the order.” Suddenly a high-resolution simulated 3D figure appeared on the screen: a girl in a white nightdress, seemingly floating in the air, her long hair waving, her smile bright. The contrast with the crude interface was striking, like a full-HD beautiful girl from a PS3 suddenly appearing on an old Nintendo console. Parsi leaned back for an instant, as if trying to escape the force of her beauty.
He pressed Esc instinctively, the emergency command to terminate remote control.
He thought he'd been hacked, but immediately realized that was impossible. He was a god-level being now. Who could invade a god's temple?

Esc failed. As the beautiful girl bowed, the whole page went black, leaving only the dark-red download bar at ninety-eight percent. But instead of advancing, it rapidly retreated. Parsi reached for the cable connecting the hard-drive array, but it was too late. The bar dropped to zero. Everything downloaded had been remotely wiped. The white card popped out of its slot.
He had been denied.

He felt a shadow falling over him. Before coming, they had thoroughly researched the college and gathered vast amounts of information. Moreover, they reported directly to the Board of Trustees and thought they knew the campus well enough. But from the moment he entered and met the legendary vice principal, unknown things hidden in the dark had begun to emerge. He was surrounded and had to break out.
Parsi sat in the dark thinking for several minutes, then picked up the white card and rushed out.
Chu Zihang slowly opened his eyes. A figure stood in the darkness before his hospital bed.

He watched silently, not particularly surprised. He had sensed the person's approach; the visitor hadn't tried to sneak. Only those with special permission could enter this intensive-care room, but this person clearly had none. He was like a thief who politely knocked before coming in.
“Hello. Sorry to disturb your rest. May I turn on the light?” the figure asked.
Chu Zihang nodded.

The figure switched on the bedside lamp, and Chu Zihang finally saw his face. It was beautiful and gentle, but those strangely captivating eyes made most people overlook its shape. One eye was sea-blue, the other pale gold, like a fine Persian cat's. Meeting his gaze, Chu Zihang felt he was looking at a Persian cat: quiet, docile, even friendly, yet extraordinarily perceptive.
Cats were difficult to read, and Chu Zihang couldn't decipher the man's gaze either.
“My name is Parsi. I'm the investigation team's secretary. I've come to investigate you,” the man introduced himself.
“Hello,” Chu Zihang said.

“I need a blood sample. It will help us study you.” Parsi took a vacuum syringe sealed in a plastic bag and inserted it into the back of Chu Zihang's hand. The vacuum drew one milliliter of fresh blood into the syringe. Parsi withdrew it. Throughout, he was like a conscientious doctor: professional, calm, possessing unquestionable authority, and acting entirely for your own good.

“Your performance at Six Flags was unforgettable. I hope to see something even more spectacular,” Parsi said with a smile. “Although some people want to strike you from the college rolls, those trying to protect you are powerful too. Neither side will win for the moment, so until a winner is decided, release yourself one hundred percent.” He bowed slightly. “We'll meet again. We can talk privately when there's a chance.”

Chu Zihang couldn't stop him, though he knew perfectly well his blood sample must not leave the room. The intensive-care room was monitored as closely as a prison, with steel layers in all four walls and bulletproof glass. If possible, Norma would mount an aircraft cannon improved by the Equipment Department's maniacs at the door and pour bullets weighing dozens of kilograms at anyone without permission. Yet the young man named Parsi had walked in as casually as that, encountering no obstacle. Chu Zihang could hardly grab Parsi, pin him to the hospital bed, and shout for the guards.
Strangely, he felt no resistance to Parsi, not only because the young man was as gentle as a cat, but because he vaguely gave off an air of 'we're the same kind of person.'
Stranger still, at first glance you felt it was Caesar standing there, though they looked nothing alike.
When the first sunlight entered the central control room, every member of the News Department looked as gray as a beaten dog, but their eyes shone like stars.

They would be legends in the history of paparazzi. Under their great leader Fingel, they had smashed through every lower limit. WikiLeaks, the paparazzi car chase involving Diana: beside their magnificent achievements tonight, all would be trivial rubbish! The News Department working at full capacity reached far beyond the college. They had close ties with major media outlets, and under the vice principal's personal guidance and earnest instruction, the team firmly believed news could change the world. They had long since accumulated vast media resources; tonight, years of preparation had been unleashed.
They were confident they could give the investigators a great surprise... or perhaps make them furious... or even reduce them to sobs...
Fingel swept out an arm. “We're done! Take everything we brought! But not a scrap of paper or any storage device leaves this room! Not one word about tonight gets out!”
“Understood!”
Fingel looked down and suddenly froze. A file had been pulled up by accident from a confidential college folder: 'Bloodline Records.'

He looked furtively around, humming a tune as he quietly pressed Print. Then, eyes turned heavenward and hands tucked into his back pockets, he sauntered to the printer and discreetly rolled the printed document into his pocket.
“Damn it! How could that secretary enter intensive care without us knowing? Who gave him access?” Abandoning his usual composure, the vice principal paced furiously like a bear robbed of its honey.

That morning word had come from intensive care: a nurse had met the investigation team's secretary at the door and had a friendly chat with him. He said he had come to take a blood sample and asked her to inform the vice principal.

“How should I know? My college clearance is exactly the same as yours. I can even find out what sleazy websites you've visited, but I couldn't find any record of the secretary entering intensive care either. That room is sealed with electronic locks, and Norma controls every one.” Anjou poured himself gin, added ice and lemon, and made a simple dry martini.
“You're normally the one who flies into a rage, yet you're this calm. I take it the blood sample the secretary took can't threaten us.” The vice principal looked surprised.

Anjou sat in the sofa and drank deeply from his martini. “I told you I'd handle the blood sample. We arranged an operation to exchange Chu Zihang's blood; his whole supply was washed several times. For the next few months his marrow won't produce enough new blood of sufficient purity. No matter how they test the sample, they won't find a problem, because it isn't his blood at all.”
“So you did get something done while your 'sore throat' was acting up. One of life's greatest blessings is having an ally who isn't a pig.” The vice principal breathed a sigh of relief.
“The real sample of Chu Zihang's blood.” Anjou handed him a sealed quartz-glass tube. “As an ardent enthusiast of alchemy, I thought you'd be interested.”

“This is blood? Are you sure you didn't mix it up with Coke?” The vice principal held it to the light. No one would believe it was blood. It was pale black, with tiny bubbles forming, joining, and bursting inside, just like Coke in a glass bottle.

“It was bright red when first drawn. It changed to this within minutes. A trace of human blood remained in the sample container and reacted with Chu Zihang's blood,” Anjou said. “The reaction was quite violent; it took some new Equipment Department devices to suppress it. This blood is too active. It's stable only inside Chu Zihang's body. In other words, he's its only vessel.”

“We certainly can't let the Board of Trustees get this. It wouldn't even need to go to a laboratory. Mix in a little ordinary human blood and the problem would be obvious.” The vice principal held the sample up in admiration. “A miracle of alchemy! A hybrid used his own body as a vessel for a highly advanced alchemical experiment, refining his blood to bring it closer to dragon blood! I'm almost moved by such reckless devotion to research!”
“You're right about reckless. We can't tell when his blood will cross the critical blood threshold. Blood amplification has already seriously harmed his body.” Anjou frowned.
The vice principal nodded. “Lend me your folding knife.”
Anjou drew it from his sleeve and handed it over. The vice principal promptly seized his wrist, flicked the knife open, and cut his finger!
“Now I'll borrow a little blood.” The vice principal withdrew the knife with a drop on it.
Anjou pressed the cut to stop the bleeding. “Couldn't you use your own blood?”
“Obviously not. It hurts,” the vice principal said frankly. He squeezed a drop of the Coke-like black blood from the quartz tube onto the blade as well.

The two drops rolled on the blade like fighters driven into an arena, slowly approaching, touching, and springing apart. The vice principal flicked his wrist, sending them along the edge to collide at the tip. They merged and left the blade.

Blood-red suddenly burst in the air, like an ethereal, seductive, coldly beautiful flower blooming and withering in an instant. The red flower turned black as ink and fell on the carpet, burning a mark the size of a coffee cup and saucer. The little room smelled of scorched wool.
“The carpet's wool. Damn it, this stuff corrodes anything that was once alive and still contains genetic material.” The vice principal was startled. “It's practically aqua regia!”
“No. It's refining nitroglycerin in your own veins!” Anjou said quietly.
“We must stop him from continuing to use that skill, or the damage will be irreversible.” The vice principal wiped the remaining blood from the blade with a tissue and returned it to Anjou.

In the Lionheart Society's clubroom, all the officers gathered under Vice President Lancelot. This was the greatest challenge in the society's history: its president would be sent before the college's internal court. The society quickly agreed to support him wholeheartedly. That wasn't difficult. Under pressure from Caesar's Student Council, the college's oldest fraternity risked slipping into second place. The reason it could still sit securely at the top was Chu Zihang. Without its super-A-rank president, the Lionheart Society had no chance against a Student Council with A-rank Caesar and Chen Motong as well as S-rank Lu Mingfei.
Though that S-rank was now sitting among them, looking as indignant as the rest.

But the killers under Chu Zihang plainly had no experience with hearings. If the same thing had happened to Caesar, the Student Council's girls in lacy white dresses and its scheming followers would all have mobilized to build support across campus. Lancelot could only lead the officers in waiting for news.
The door opened. Fingel came in, sat on the sofa, and let out a long breath. “Done! No problem at all!”
After a moment's silence, the killers applauded in relief.

Lancelot handed Fingel an envelope containing a promissory note drawn on the Lionheart Society's emergency funds. Fingel accepted it without hesitation, taking money from the principal on one side and the society on the other. The vice principal would have done the same.
“Leave the hearing to me. If I take your money, I'll solve your troubles.” Fingel was full of confidence. “If you have time, why not visit Chu Zihang instead of sitting here looking miserable?”

Lancelot sprang up. Only now did the Frenchman remember they still hadn't visited Chu Zihang. While Chu Zihang was unconscious, no visitors had been allowed in intensive care, although the freshman Xia Mi had received special access from the principal. Today was the first day visits were permitted. All the Lionheart Society officers followed Lancelot out, discussing in the corridor what sort of bouquet to prepare.
Lu Mingfei tried to follow, but Fingel patted his shoulder from behind. “I have bad news. Want to hear it?” His eyebrows drooped.
“Damn it, better to die sooner and be reborn sooner. Tell me!” Lu Mingfei didn't take it seriously. When had his useless senior ever had good news?
Fingel handed him a tissue. “Get ready, junior. You can start wiping your tears when you've heard.”
“Bah! This looks like a decent tissue. I'll save it to wipe my mouth at dinner.” Lu Mingfei folded it and tucked it into his pocket.

Fingel gave him a thumbs-up and bared his teeth. “Junior, your spirit knows no bounds. If you can still think of dinner no matter how hard you've been hit, your fighting spirit is intact! Listen carefully...” He licked his lips. “Caesar proposed to Nono!”
Lu Mingfei stared for a moment, then smiled.
Everything around his ears seemed blank. He felt nothing, not the least bit sad. He must have heard wrong, he thought.

He must have heard wrong. Don't believe rumors. In a minute the mistake would be corrected and everything would return to its former course. Caesar and Nono were still boyfriend and girlfriend, but things between them were a little complicated. They hadn't even graduated; why get married? A campus tyrant like Principal Anjou would scold them and tell them studies came first! What marriage? Wait until graduation! That would give him a few more years to moon over her. Damn it, wasn't college about mooning over the prettiest girl in school or class until the flower fell, the water cooled, the dust settled, and the beauty married a rich heir, at which point you grew up? It was a process! Did those two understand the beauty of the process? Couldn't they stop rushing it? If you rushed it... some people who hadn't had time to grow up would be very sad...
Even knowing he couldn't change the ending, couldn't he be allowed a tiny, disreputable crush before the dust settled?
Lu Mingfei stared at Fingel. He didn't know how much time passed before Fingel nodded vigorously and raised three fingers to the sky, swearing a curse on himself if he'd made it up.

At last Lu Mingfei felt sad: utter powerlessness, his heart too lazy even to beat, an awful sensation between exhaustion and pain spreading through his body. He wanted to sink slowly into a crouch, or simply lie on the floor and stop moving.
He forced himself to hold on and stared at Fingel. “Damn. How would you know?”

“Anyone at the college who wants to marry has to apply and undergo bloodline analysis, so they don't produce descendants with unstable bloodlines.” Fingel pulled out a crumpled printout. “From the college's bloodline records. I happened across it in the Central Control Room. I thought, damn, isn't that hard on my brother? So I secretly printed a copy and brought it out. I'm a good friend, right?”

Lu Mingfei unfolded the paper: 'Application to Marry A-Rank Student Chen Motong (Student No. A09003),' applicant Caesar Gattuso. It was an old-fashioned document, probably copied from some template Caesar had found. It chiefly contained his and Nono's résumés, when they met, the state of their relationship, and their laudable wish to combine excellent bloodlines and raise exceptional offspring. Attached was a report from the college's genetic science department stating that, based on blood samples, Caesar and Chen Motong's children were very unlikely to have unstable genes. The paperwork looked complete. If the investigation team hadn't suddenly targeted the principal and suspended all college procedures, the application might already have been approved.
It was like needing an organization's approval to marry in 1950s China. Lu Mingfei found the document both funny and frightening.
“The tissue... still saving it to wipe your mouth?” Fingel asked cautiously.

Lu Mingfei looked down at the tissue in his pocket, instinctively wiped his mouth with it, and tossed it on the floor. Who did Fingel think he was? The hero of a tragedy, lifting his face forty-five degrees to shed tears into the wind? He was just an extra. An extra didn't need a tearful profile. The whole affair had nothing to do with him anyway.
“I'm fine. I'm going to take a leak,” Lu Mingfei said.

He turned and walked out, taking one step after another under Fingel's gaze. His back was slightly bent, his shoulders heavy, his arms hanging limply and growing heavier. He thought he had to walk faster or his arms would drag on the ground before he reached the end of the corridor. Then in Fingel's eyes he'd look either like Imperial Uncle Liu... or a monkey robbed of its bananas...
At last he made it to the end of the corridor. He turned the corner and ran, bursting into an empty restroom.

He leaned against the door and slowly sat down on the floor, remembering everything between him and Nono. So many messy little things: Nono ordering him to run errands for the Student Council's sailing practice, ordering him to buy a blueberry egg tart for a late-night snack, ordering him to remember how she took her coffee, 'a latte with one sugar.' Trivial, meaningless episodes. If he picked out the essence, there was very little...
“Now that's our Ricardo M. Lu.” In the small cinema auditorium, before dozens of Literature Club members, Nono patted his face with a smile he couldn't tell was tender or teasing.
“It's beautiful... whoever sent it.” Nono stood beside him, watching the fireworks slowly fade in the night sky.

“Don't die!” He shouted in the bitterly cold waters of the Three Gorges, holding a girl who didn't belong to him. Nono's dark-red hair drifted like thick seaweed, and she wore a bikini that set his blood racing. Yet at the time he had felt his blood was about to freeze. His whole body was cold, and he was only afraid she would die... If she died, he would be lonely again...

Lu Mingze said he was lonely, but he really didn't think so. By day he could moon over a pretty senior; at night he could eat late-night snacks and shoot the breeze with his useless senior. What was lonely about that?
If the world could stay that way forever, it wouldn't be bad.

Perhaps it was a little greedy to want everyone to remain as they had been when he first met them... Chen Wenwen should be on a sunny bench reading Marguerite Duras's The Lover, melancholy over a sad story that had nothing to do with her; his useless senior should never graduate, so they could share a room, eat late-night snacks every evening, and say whatever was in their hearts, good or ridiculous; Nono would always be that imperious little red-haired witch driving a Ferrari, fiercely mischievous and full of wicked ideas, marriage still in her distant future. She wouldn't have learned to cook yet, would stubbornly love ice cream nearly the color of her hair, and would race with him along a dark mountain road...
But things would change. Everyone would leave, and he would remain where he was.
He raised his head and rubbed his dejected face in the mirror.
